messages.subject: get.global.climate() layers
parts:
Hello,

Is there a list/documentation detailing what the 97 different layers correspond to when downloading the global climate data using:

get.global.climate()

From what I can see, the original CRU dataset has substantially fewer layers than 97. CRU v1 has 11 layers (https://crudata.uea.ac.uk/~timm/grid/CRU_CL_1_0.html) and CRU v2 has 8 layers. Even when adding cloud cover and aerosol layers, I can't work out how this totals 97.

Many thanks,

Simon

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: get.global.climate() layers
parts:
Hi Simon,

They are per month. If you look in the code for the micro_global function you'll see what's pasted below which should tell you what you need to know (ALTT is elevation). The function 'build_global_climate' creates it from scratch. I'll add some documentation to the package so it's a bit more obvious (and note the divisions by 10 to get the values into the right units - they are stored in integer form in the data set to keep the file size down).

All the best,
Mike

        global_climate <- raster::brick(paste(folder, "/global_climate.nc", 
            sep = ""))
        CLIMATE <- raster::extract(global_climate, x)
        ALTT <- as.numeric(CLIMATE[, 1])
        RAINFALL <- CLIMATE[, 2:13]
        RAINYDAYS <- CLIMATE[, 14:25]/10
        WNMAXX <- CLIMATE[, 26:37]/10
        WNMINN <- WNMAXX * 0.1
        TMINN <- CLIMATE[, 38:49]/10
        TMAXX <- CLIMATE[, 50:61]/10
        ALLMINTEMPS <- TMINN
        ALLMAXTEMPS <- TMAXX
        ALLTEMPS <- cbind(ALLMAXTEMPS, ALLMINTEMPS)
        RHMINN <- CLIMATE[, 62:73]/10
        RHMAXX <- CLIMATE[, 74:85]/10
        CCMINN <- CLIMATE[, 86:97]/10

parts:
Hi Mike,

I have another question regarding the above, I'm hoping you can help if that's okay! 

I'm curious as to why RAINYDAYS has been divided by 10 when using micro_global. From looking at the source code for build.global.climate(), there are two variables which aren't multiplied by 10 (to convert from CRUs original decimal values to integer). That's precipitation and rain day frequency. In the above code, rainfall hasn't been divided by 10 (as it was never multiplied by 10 in within build.global.climate) whereas rainy days has, even though it's already in decimal form. Is this intended? If so, would it be possible to explain why this is the case? I'd have thought that RAINYDAYS would not be divided by 10 in this instance.

For example (code from build.global.climate):

else {
                for (j in 1:12) { 
                  if (i == 2 | i == 3) { 
                    global_climate[[1 + (i - 2) * 12 + j]] <- round(raster::rasterize(x, gridout, data[, 2 + j]), 0) 
                  }

                  else {
                    global_climate[[1 + (i - 2) * 12 + j]] <- round(raster::rasterize(x, gridout, data[, 2 + j]) * 10, 0) 
                  }
                  cat(paste(vars[i], " month ", j, " done \n", sep = ""))
                }
            }
        }


where i = 2 is precipitation and i = 3 is rd0 (or wet day frequency).

Many thanks for your time,
Simon

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: get.global.climate() layers
parts:
Hi Simon,

You're correct. Good spotting! I had originally multiplied the rainy days variable by 10 but later realised that it wasn't necessary as it was an integer data set. The global climate data set that 'get.global.climate' downloads, however, did have the rainy days multiplied by 10. I will replace that file with one identical to what build.global.climate produces and modify the code for micro_global accordingly in the next release.

Thanks for pointing this out.

All the best,
Mike
